title: Computer Architecture & Mechanical Sympathy
summary: The hardware has rules. Respect how the CPU and memory really work and the same algorithm can run 10x faster — that awareness is mechanical sympathy.

blocks.markdown:
Modern CPUs don't run your code line-by-line; they overlap, reorder, and guess ahead.

- The CPU is **fast**; memory is **slow**. The whole game is keeping the core fed with nearby data.
- Data moves in **64-byte cache lines**, never single bytes — so *layout* matters as much as *amount*.
- **Sequential, contiguous, predictable = fast.** The hardware prefetches and predicts for you.
- **Mechanical sympathy** is writing code that works *with* the hardware, not against it.

blocks.subTitle: The hidden cost cliffs
blocks.markdown:
Two latencies dominate everything: missing cache and mispredicting a branch.

| Event | Rough cost |
|---|---|
| Add / multiply | ~1 cycle |
| Branch misprediction | ~15-20 cycles |
| L1 cache hit | ~1 ns |
| DRAM miss | ~100 ns (~100x L1) |

An add is cheap; a DRAM round-trip dwarfs it. If an O(n) loop is mysteriously slow, suspect cache misses, not the math.

blocks.subTitle: Executing one instruction
blocks.markdown:
An instruction runs in stages, and the core overlaps many at once.

- Classic five stages: **fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back**.
- A **pipeline** overlaps them, so throughput nears one instruction per cycle even though each still takes five.
- Real cores are **superscalar** (several instructions started per cycle) and **out-of-order** (run when inputs are ready, retire in program order).
- You never see the reordering — but you feel its absence when dependencies force a wait.

blocks.subTitle: Branch prediction
blocks.markdown:
A conditional branch is a fork the CPU can't afford to wait on, so it **guesses**.

- The **branch predictor** uses history; modern ones hit **90-99%** on typical code.
- A right guess is free. A wrong guess **flushes** the pipeline: a **~15-20 cycle** penalty.
- **Predictable** branches (loop conditions, almost-always-taken) cost nothing.
- **Random** data (50/50, no pattern) mispredicts half the time and can dominate a hot loop.
- Classic demo: summing elements over a threshold is several times faster on a **sorted** array — same code, predictable branch.

blocks.subTitle: Cache hierarchy & cache lines
blocks.markdown:
Memory is a hierarchy: small-fast on top, big-slow below, each level a cache for the next.

- Order checked: **L1 → L2 → L3 → DRAM**, stopping at the first **hit**; a full miss is a DRAM round-trip.
- L1/L2 are **private per core**; **L3 is shared**.
- Memory moves in **64-byte cache lines** — reading one `int` pulls in ~16 neighbors.
- Great for **sequential** access, wasteful for **random** access.
- A **hardware prefetcher** watches your pattern and grabs the next line early.

blocks.subTitle: The latency cliffs
blocks.markdown:
Each level down is a step-change, not a smooth slope.

| Level | Latency | ~Cycles |
|---|---|---|
| Register | ~0.3 ns | ~1 |
| L1 | ~1 ns | ~3-4 |
| L3 | ~12 ns | ~40 |
| DRAM | ~100 ns | ~250-300 |

The **DRAM cliff** (~100x L1) is the one most code trips over. If your working set fits in L3 you fly; spill to DRAM and you crawl. See [complexity-big-o](complexity-big-o) on why constants matter.

blocks.subTitle: Pipeline hazards
blocks.markdown:
Three things stall a pipeline — and one is often invisible.

- **Structural** — two instructions want the same unit. Rare on modern chips.
- **Data** — instruction 2 needs instruction 1's result. **Forwarding** hides most, but a long **dependency chain** serializes everything.
- **Control** — a branch whose direction isn't known yet; solved by prediction.

A dependency chain stalls even with **zero cache misses**: each step waits on the last, so the pipeline can't overlap. Break it (e.g. multiple accumulators) to restore parallelism.

blocks.subTitle: The levers you trade on
blocks.markdown:
Mechanical sympathy is a set of trades, not a single rule.

- **Locality vs flexibility** — contiguous arrays are cache-fast but rigid; pointer structures are flexible but cache-hostile.
- **Predictability vs branchiness** — sort or group data to make a branch free before reaching for branchless tricks.
- **Footprint vs cache fit** — compact data that fits in cache often beats a fancier algorithm that spills to DRAM.
- **Parallelism vs contention** — more threads help only if they don't fight over cache lines or locks.

blocks.subTitle: Array vs linked list
blocks.markdown:
Same Big-O, wildly different speed — choose by access pattern.

| Aspect | Array | Linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | Contiguous | Scattered |
| Prefetch | Yes | No |
| Traversal | Bandwidth-bound | Latency-bound |

Arrays win 10-100x on real iteration. Reach for a list only when you need stable addresses or O(1) splicing of known nodes ([linked-lists](linked-lists)).

blocks.subTitle: Data layout wins
blocks.markdown:
You rarely write assembly, but your data layout decides cache behavior.

- **Arrays over linked lists** in hot loops — spatial locality and prefetching beat pointer-chasing.
- **Struct-of-arrays (SoA)** — if a loop touches only the `x` field, store all `x`s contiguously so each line is 100% useful; it also **vectorizes** better.
- **Hot/cold splitting** — keep frequently-used fields together so hot lines stay dense.
- **SIMD** — one wide instruction processes 4-16 values at once; compilers auto-vectorize flat, dependency-free numeric loops.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & signals
blocks.markdown:
These ideas run the systems you use — and show up as concrete metrics.

- **LMAX Disruptor** — a padded, pre-allocated ring buffer hit 6M+ ops/sec by designing for the cache, not Big-O.
- **ScyllaDB / shared-nothing** — one thread per core, no cross-core shared state, to dodge coherence traffic.
- **Columnar DBs** (ClickHouse, Parquet, Arrow) — SoA at storage scale; scans read only needed columns ([storage-systems](storage-systems)).
- **Profiler signals**: low **IPC** (under 1) means stalls; high **LLC miss rate** means fix layout; double-digit **branch-miss** means an unpredictable branch.

blocks.subTitle: False sharing
blocks.markdown:
You parallelize a counter across N threads and it gets *slower*. That's false sharing.

- Two cores write two distinct variables that unluckily sit on the **same 64-byte line**.
- Cache coherence tracks ownership **per line**, so each write invalidates the other core's copy — the line **ping-pongs** between caches.
- Neither variable is truly shared, yet every write pays cache-miss latency.
- **Fix**: pad each hot per-thread variable to its own line (`alignas(64)`, Java `@Contended`, padding bytes). Ties into [concurrency-parallelism](concurrency-parallelism).

blocks.subTitle: Common misconceptions
blocks.markdown:
The beliefs that cost you 100x in production:

- **"Big-O is all that matters."** The DRAM-vs-cache gap *is* a ~100x constant; two O(n) loops can differ 100x.
- **"The CPU runs my code in order."** It pipelines, runs superscalar, out-of-order, and speculates past branches.
- **"Linked lists are great for inserts."** O(1) only with a node pointer; finding the spot is a cache-missing traversal.
- **"More threads = more speed."** Only without contention — false sharing can make N threads slower than one.
- **"All branches are cheap."** A *predictable* one is; an unpredictable one in a hot loop costs ~15-20 cycles each.
